title: GATE CS Topic Test — Compiler Design (Set 2)
titleEn: GATE CS Topic Test — Compiler Design (Set 2)

questions.questionTextEn: What is the minimum number of temporary variables required to translate `x = (a + b) * (c + d) - (e + f)` into three-address code if temporary variables CANNOT be reused?
questions.explanationEn: The 5 binary operations compile to `t1 = a + b`, `t2 = c + d`, `t3 = t1 * t2`, `t4 = e + f`, and `x = t3 - t4`. Since the final subtraction assigns directly to `x`, only 4 temporary variables are needed.

questions.questionTextEn: In standard C grammar, if `a = 10, b = 4, c = 2`, what is the value of `a - b - c` given left-to-right associativity of subtraction?
questions.explanationEn: Left-associative grouping gives `(10 - 4) - 2 = 6 - 2 = 4`.

questions.questionTextEn: Which phase of a compiler is primarily responsible for grouping characters from the source program into meaningful tokens and stripping whitespace and comments?
questions.explanationEn: The Lexical Analyzer (scanner) reads the character stream, removes comments/whitespace, and produces a stream of tokens using finite automata.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following instructions is ALWAYS a 'leader' (the first instruction of a basic block) in three-address code?
optionsEn: The instruction immediately preceding a jump
The target of any conditional or unconditional jump
questions.explanationEn: Leaders are: (1) the first instruction of the program, (2) any instruction that is the target of a jump, and (3) any instruction immediately following a jump.

questions.questionTextEn: Global register allocation via Chaitin's algorithm models register assignment as:
optionsEn: Graph coloring of the variable interference graph
Minimum spanning tree of the CFG
questions.explanationEn: Two variables interfere (have an edge) if they are simultaneously live at some program point; assigning `k` registers corresponds to `k`-coloring the interference graph.

questions.questionTextEn:
In a basic block containing:
1. `a = b + c`
2. `d = a * 2`
3. `b = d - 1`
Suppose ONLY `b` is live at the exit of the block. How many variables are live immediately BEFORE instruction 1?
questions.explanationEn: Backward trace: after 3: `{b}`. Before 3: `{d}`. Before 2: `{a}`. Before 1: `{b, c}` (since `a` is defined in 1, and `b, c` are used). Total = 2 variables (`b` and `c`).

questions.questionTextEn: A program has 4 variables `a, b, c, d`. At point 1, `{a, b, c}` are simultaneously live; at point 2, `{b, c, d}` are simultaneously live; `a` and `d` are never live together. What is the minimum number of registers needed to allocate all 4 variables without spilling?
questions.explanationEn: The interference graph has triangles `{a, b, c}` and `{b, c, d}`, with no edge between `a` and `d`. Thus `a` and `d` can share register R1, while `b` gets R2 and `c` gets R3. Minimum = 3 registers.

questions.questionTextEn: In an L-attributed SDD, an inherited attribute of symbol `X_j` in production `A -> X_1 X_2 ... X_n` may depend ONLY on:
optionsEn: Inherited attributes of A and attributes of symbols X_1, ..., X_{j-1} to its left
Synthesized attributes of X_{j+1}, ..., X_n to its right
Attributes of any symbol in the production
questions.explanationEn: L-attributed (left-to-right) definitions allow inherited attributes to flow from the parent `A` and from siblings strictly to the left (`X_1..X_{j-1}`), enabling single-pass left-to-right evaluation.

questions.questionTextEn: In an S-attributed Syntax-Directed Definition (SDD), all attributes are:
questions.explanationEn: An S-attributed SDD uses exclusively synthesized attributes (computed bottom-up from children's attributes) and can always be evaluated during LR parsing.

questions.questionTextEn: For the grammar `S -> a S b | ε`, how many symbols are in `FOLLOW(S)`?
questions.explanationEn: `$` is in `FOLLOW(S)` because `S` is the start symbol, and `b` is in `FOLLOW(S)` from `S -> a S b`. Thus `FOLLOW(S) = {$, b}` — 2 symbols.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following parameter-passing mechanisms allow a called function `f(x)` to modify the caller's actual variable passed as `x`?
questions.explanationEn: Call by Reference modifies the caller's variable directly; Call by Value-Result copies the modified local back upon return; Call by Name substitutes the lvalue directly. Call by Value only modifies a local copy (A is false).

questions.questionTextEn: Which memory allocation strategy is required to support recursive function calls in a programming language?
optionsEn: Stack-based dynamic allocation of activation records
questions.explanationEn: Recursive calls have multiple simultaneous active invocations of the same function, each needing its own private locals and return address, which stack allocation naturally provides.

questions.questionTextEn:
Consider the production `A -> B C` with semantic rules:
1. `B.i = A.i + 1`
2. `C.i = B.s + A.i`
3. `A.s = B.s + C.s`
(where `.i` denotes inherited and `.s` denotes synthesized attributes). This SDD is:
questions.explanationEn: It uses inherited attributes (`B.i`, `C.i`), so it is NOT S-attributed. Each inherited attribute depends only on parent `A.i` and left sibling `B.s` (never on right siblings), so it IS L-attributed.

questions.questionTextEn: A recursive function `f(n)` allocates an activation record of 64 bytes per call and calls `f(n - 1)` down to base case `f(0)` (which does not recurse further). What is the peak stack memory (in bytes) consumed during the call `f(9)`?
questions.explanationEn: Active frames at peak depth are `f(9), f(8), ..., f(0)` — 10 frames total. Peak stack usage = `10 × 64 = 640` bytes.

questions.questionTextEn:
Consider the SDD:
`E -> E1 + T { E.val = E1.val * T.val }`
`E -> T { E.val = T.val }`
`T -> T1 * F { T.val = T1.val + F.val }`
`T -> F { T.val = F.val }`
`F -> num { F.val = num.val }`
What is the value of `E.val` for the input `2 + 3 * 4`?
questions.explanationEn: Notice the grammar still gives `*` higher precedence than `+`, while the semantic actions swap `+` and `*`! Parse tree is `2 + (3 * 4)`. `T(3 * 4)` evaluates `3 + 4 = 7`. Then `E(2 + 7)` evaluates `2 * 7 = 14`.

Constant propagation substitutes `a=5`, constant folding evaluates `5+3=8` and `8*2=16`, and dead code elimination removes the now-unused assignments to `a`, `b`, and `c`. Register spilling is unrelated (D is false).

questions.questionTextEn:
Consider the grammar:
`E -> T E'`
`E' -> + T E' | ε`
`T -> F T'`
`T' -> * F T' | ε`
`F -> ( E ) | id`
How many symbols (including `$`) are in `FOLLOW(F)`?
questions.explanationEn: From `T -> F T'`, `FIRST(T') - {ε} = {*}` is in `FOLLOW(F)`. Since `T' =>* ε`, `FOLLOW(T)` is also in `FOLLOW(F)`. `FOLLOW(T)` contains `+` (from `FIRST(E')`) and `FOLLOW(E) = {$, )}`. Thus `FOLLOW(F) = {*, +, ), $}` — 4 symbols.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements about Basic Blocks are TRUE?
optionsEn: Control can enter a basic block only at its first instruction (the leader)
Control can leave a basic block only at its last instruction
A basic block can contain a conditional branch instruction in the middle of the block
Every instruction in a basic block executes the exact same number of times (assuming no exceptions)
questions.explanationEn: Basic blocks are single-entry, single-exit straight-line sequences (A, B, D). A branch instruction always terminates a basic block, so it cannot appear in the middle (C is false).

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements about transforming grammars for top-down parsing are TRUE?
optionsEn: Eliminating left recursion replaces left-recursive rules with right-recursive rules while preserving the language
Left factoring defers the choice between productions sharing a common prefix
Left factoring always makes any grammar LL(1)
Indirect left recursion (`A -> Bα, B -> Aβ`) must also be eliminated for LL(1) parsing
questions.explanationEn: A, B, and D are true. Left factoring removes common-prefix conflicts, but an ambiguous or non-LL(1) grammar still cannot become LL(1) (C is false).
`g()` passes its local `a = 10` as argument `b = 10` to `f`. Inside `f`, the free variable `a` resolves lexically to global `a = 3`. Hence `f(10)` returns `3 + 10 = 13`.
